strengths: Well-motivated clinical challenge: The paper targets a critical and practical issue in clinical NLP, specifically that off-the-shelf LLM text rewriting and augmentation frequently drop key medical facts or introduce hallucinations, which can compromise the integrity of downstream medical models.

Comprehensive experimental scope: The authors evaluate across multiple downstream clinical tasks (30-day readmission, in-hospital mortality, length-of-stay), zero/few-shot evaluations (patient phenotyping, ICD code retrieval), and augmentation quality metrics (preservation rate, hallucination rate).

Interesting exploration of single-model distillation: The extension evaluating whether dual-model guidance can be distilled into a single model via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) provides useful practical insights into foundation model post-training for domain augmentation.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The proposed 'query-based model collaboration' essentially runs an off-the-shelf clinical NER model (DistilBERT-based) to extract medical entities and inserts them into an LLM prompt as a verbatim preservation constraint ('Preserve the following tokens: ...'). Keyword-preserving paraphrasing and entity-constrained generation are well-established paradigms in NLP, making the methodological contribution quite incremental.

Circular evaluation of synthetic data quality: As acknowledged in Appendix A.3, the evaluation of Preservation Rate (PR) and Hallucination Rate (HR) relies on 'the same tool used to create $K_i$' (the weak expert NER model). This introduces severe circular evaluation bias: the metric measures fidelity with respect to the weak expert's own predictions rather than an independent gold-standard or clinician-adjudicated review.

Unclear filtering thresholds and potential baseline disadvantage: In Appendix A.3, the authors state that a generated note is accepted 'only when PR meets or exceeds $\tau_{PR}$ and HR is at or below $\tau_{HR}$', and that retrieval samples are discarded if label-defining entities fail to appear. However, the exact values of $\tau_{PR}$ and $\tau_{HR}$, the acceptance/rejection rates, and whether baselines (Naive, CATO) underwent comparable rejection sampling or filtering are not specified, introducing confounding factors into the empirical comparisons.

Suboptimal evaluation metrics for imbalanced clinical benchmarks: In Table 2, in-hospital mortality and 30-day readmission are evaluated using standard Accuracy. In datasets like MIMIC-III, mortality and readmission are highly class-imbalanced (mortality rate is typically ~10%), where naive majority-class prediction achieves ~90% accuracy. Standard benchmarks in this domain evaluate AUROC and AUPRC (PR-AUC) or macro-F1 to measure true predictive utility.

Draft quality and inconsistencies in the appendix: Section A.3 contains unedited drafting artifacts (e.g., headings such as 'Training details – add details on SFT and DPO') and verbatim copy-pasting of sentences across subsections, indicating that the appendix was not thoroughly polished.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Addressing hallucinations and information distortion during LLM-based data augmentation in high-stakes domains such as healthcare is a critical challenge.

Conceptually simple and accessible approach: Guiding an instruction-tuned LLM via explicit entity preservation constraints extracted by a lightweight domain NER model is computationally practical and does not necessarily require costly LLM pre-training or fine-tuning.

Broad range of experimental settings: The empirical study evaluates multiple tasks including clinical outcome prediction (readmission, mortality, length-of-stay), patient phenotyping, and zero-shot ICD code retrieval, and includes an exploratory extension distilling the behavior via DPO.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic and methodological originality: The proposed framework essentially chains an off-the-shelf NER model (DistilBERT biomedical-ner-all) to extract clinical entities and inserts them into an LLM prompt as verbatim constraints. While framed using causal terminology (causal graph G, domain variables V vs. spurious variables U), the work does not propose new causal algorithms or constrained generation architectures beyond standard prompt-level instruction.

Circular evaluation of text quality metrics: The synthetic text evaluation metrics (Preservation Rate and Hallucination Rate in Section 5.3 and A.3) extract entities using the exact same NER tool used to generate the constraint set Ki. Because the generator is explicitly prompted to retain Ki, evaluating success with the same model creates an intrinsic circular bias and ignores the NER tool's own false positives and omissions.

Inadequate evaluation metrics for imbalanced clinical benchmarks: For highly imbalanced clinical prediction tasks like 30-day readmission and in-hospital mortality on MIMIC-III, standard literature practices require AUROC and AUPRC. Reporting only raw classification accuracy can be misleading (e.g., predicting the negative class alone on mortality often yields ~90% accuracy). Furthermore, differences in mortality accuracy between 'None' (0.911 ± 0.04) and 'Ours' (0.917 ± 0.02) are within standard error margins.

Lack of essential experimental and cohort details: The manuscript lacks key specifications regarding cohort selection, patient-level train/validation/test splits, cohort size, and class distributions for MIMIC-III. Additionally, while Section A.3 mentions filtering candidates using acceptance thresholds tau_PR and tau_HR, the exact numerical thresholds used in experiments are never reported.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: mitigating hallucinations and preserving clinical facts during LLM-based textual data augmentation in healthcare.
Evaluates on multiple clinical tasks and downstream regimes on MIMIC-III, including 30-day readmission, in-hospital mortality, length-of-stay, zero/few-shot phenotyping, and ICD retrieval.
Explores an interesting extension in Section 5.4, investigating whether inference-time collaborative guidance can be distilled into a single model using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty and conceptual overclaiming: The proposed 'query-based model collaboration' framework is essentially a standard prompting constraint where an off-the-shelf NER model (DistilBERT) extracts entity spans, which are then injected into an LLM prompt with the instruction 'preserve these tokens verbatim'. Framing this standard pipeline as a formal causally-driven multi-model collaboration overstates the technical contribution, as no formal causal identification, invariant risk minimization, or structural causal modeling is actually performed.

Circularity and bias in safety evaluation metrics: In Section 5.3 and Appendix A.3, Preservation Rate (PR) and Hallucination Rate (HR) are computed using the exact same NER model (biomedical-ner-all) that is used to generate the constraint set Ki. Because the generator is explicitly prompted with tokens produced by this specific extractor, evaluating against the same extractor creates a self-fulfilling circular evaluation. There is no independent clinical validation, physician review, or cross-tool verification (e.g., MetaMap, cTAKES, or alternative clinical LLMs).

Hidden acceptance filtering and discrepancy between main text and appendix: Appendix A.3 reveals a critical component that is entirely omitted from the main methodology (Section 4): 'We accept a candidate only when PR meets or exceeds tau_PR and HR is at or below tau_HR.' This reveals an unmentioned rejection-sampling step. The paper does not specify what thresholds tau_PR and tau_HR were used, what percentage of generated samples were rejected, or whether baseline methods were afforded a comparable filtering mechanism.

Incomplete baseline comparisons: The empirical comparison is restricted to unconstrained naive prompting and CATO (Feder et al., 2023). Standard and established clinical text augmentation methods—such as ontology-guided synonym replacement (e.g., UMLS/SNOMED CT), back-translation, or clinical EDA—are completely missing.

Noticeable drafting artifacts and presentation issues: Appendix A.3 contains an unedited internal drafting note as a section header: 'Training details – add details on SFT and DPO.' Furthermore, Section A.3 mostly duplicates paragraphs from Section 4 and Section 5 verbatim. There are also typographical inconsistencies in the tables (e.g., 'Pred.' instead of 'Prec.' in Table 3, and 'Period (RMSE)' instead of 'Length-of-stay (RMSE)' in Table 5).

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in clinical NLP: mitigating factual corruption and hallucinations during LLM-based data augmentation in high-stakes domains.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning both synthetic data quality (Preservation Rate and Hallucination Rate at token and UMLS concept levels) and utility across multiple downstream clinical prediction tasks (readmission, mortality, length-of-stay) and zero/few-shot evaluations (phenotyping, ICD coding).

Inclusion of clinician expert evaluation (three clinical nurses) and inter-annotator agreement metrics (Fleiss' Kappa) adds credibility to the claims of improved preservation and reduced hallucination.

Well-structured ablations exploring variations in weak expert models, generalist model sizes, evaluator NER models, as well as distillation of the collaborative pipeline via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is relatively modest; the core framework essentially consists of extracting named entities with an off-the-shelf NER model and prompting an LLM with explicit verbatim preservation constraints.

Lack of quantitative evaluation of generation diversity: Forcing verbatim preservation of all extracted clinical entities may restrict the diversity of the generated notes. Metrics such as Self-BLEU, distinct n-grams, or semantic distance relative to original notes should be reported to ensure the model produces non-trivial variations beyond superficial syntactic shifts.

Evaluation is limited to a single primary data source (MIMIC-III). Validating the framework on notes from other institutions, different EHR systems, or distinct medical subspecialties (e.g., radiology or pathology reports) would strengthen claims of generalizability across domain shifts.

Unclear filtering impact: Section A.3 mentions filtering candidates based on PR and HR thresholds (tau_PR and tau_HR), but does not report the exact threshold values, rejection rates, or how this rejection sampling impacts effective computational cost and throughput.

strengths: Relevant and well-motivated problem: General-purpose LLM text augmentation often distorts safety-critical information or hallucinates factual inaccuracies in sensitive domains such as healthcare.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates both intrinsic safety metrics (entity preservation and hallucination rates at both token and concept/UMLS levels) and extrinsic downstream utility (supervised outcome prediction, patient phenotyping, and zero-shot ICD code retrieval).

Thorough ablations and extensions: The authors evaluate multiple weak-expert models (biomedical NER vs. general NER), different generalist model sizes, investigate evaluator bias with different NER evaluators, include a preliminary human expert evaluation, analyze computational costs, and demonstrate knowledge distillation via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The core mechanism is conceptually simple—running an existing clinical NER model (biomedical-ner-all) to extract entity mentions and injecting them into an LLM prompt with instructions to preserve them verbatim. Framing this as a novel 'query-based model collaboration framework' somewhat overclaims the technical contribution.

Evaluation metric choice on imbalanced clinical tasks: For 30-day readmission and in-hospital mortality, the paper reports standard accuracy (Table 1). In clinical EHR benchmarks like MIMIC-III, in-hospital mortality and 30-day readmission are heavily class-imbalanced (mortality is typically ~10%). Reporting only classification accuracy (where a dummy majority-class baseline readily achieves ~90%) can be misleading; standard clinical NLP benchmarks rely primarily on AUROC and AUPRC.

Lack of true cross-institution out-of-distribution evaluation: The introduction motivates the framework by noting that clinical models struggle across institutions, patient populations, and documentation styles. However, the downstream experiments only train and test on splits within MIMIC-III without evaluating true out-of-distribution generalization (e.g., evaluating models trained on MIMIC-III on eICU or MIMIC-IV).

Small-scale generalist models used for augmentation: The main augmentation pipeline uses relatively small open models (Qwen-3-0.6B and LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B). It remains unclear whether larger foundation models (e.g., LLaMA-3.1-70B, GPT-4o) would suffer from the same degree of entity omission when prompted with standard clinical instructions, or if the benefit of an auxiliary NER extractor diminishes as LLM capability scales.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Addressing hallucinations and preservation of critical domain semantics in LLM-based data augmentation is crucial for safety-critical settings like healthcare.

Comprehensive experimental breadth: The paper evaluates multiple clinical tasks on MIMIC-III (30-day readmission, in-hospital mortality, length-of-stay prediction, phenotyping, and ICD coding) against multiple baselines (unconstrained LLM, CATO, biomedical LLM, rule-based substitution).

Inclusion of clinician validation and cost analysis: The authors provide human expert annotations with three clinical nurses measuring inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' Kappa), alongside an empirical runtime and GPU cost comparison.
weaknesses: Flawed evaluation metrics for clinical prediction benchmarks: MIMIC-III clinical prediction tasks such as 30-day readmission and in-hospital mortality suffer from severe class imbalance (typically ~10% positive prevalence). Reporting raw Accuracy rather than standard clinical ML metrics such as AUROC and AUPRC (or Macro-F1) renders the downstream performance results in Table 1 largely uninformative (e.g., a trivial majority-class predictor easily achieves ~90% accuracy on mortality, mirroring the reported 0.90–0.92 numbers).

Limited methodological novelty and over-claimed theoretical contribution: The proposed method fundamentally consists of running an off-the-shelf biomedical NER model (DistilBERT) and appending the extracted entity strings into an LLM prompt with instructions to preserve them verbatim. Framing this standard constrained prompting strategy as a 'novel query-based model collaboration framework' and framing a standard application of the law of total probability ($r\varepsilon + (1-r)p_c$) as a theoretical bound overstates the technical depth.

Metric circularity and unclear candidate rejection filtering: The Preservation Rate (PR) and Hallucination Rate (HR) in Table 2 are computed using the exact same NER tool used to extract the constraint keywords $K_i$. Additionally, Appendix A.3 notes that 'we accept a candidate only when PR meets or exceeds $\tau_{PR}$ and HR is at or below $\tau_{HR}$' and 'we discard any samples where the Preservation Rate falls below our threshold'. It is unclear whether baselines were subjected to identical rejection sampling, what percentage of samples were discarded, and how this filtering impacts the fairness of comparison.

Lack of diversity evaluation: Constraining all detected medical entities to be copied verbatim risks producing near-identical rewrites with only minor syntactic variations. The manuscript does not evaluate the diversity of the generated notes (e.g., via Self-BLEU, Distinct-n, or semantic distance of non-critical spans), leaving it ambiguous whether the downstream utility stems from meaningful augmentation or simple memorization of slightly perturbed templates.
